title: 12 Facts About Earth That Sound Fake (But Are 100% True)

lines.t: The ground beneath your feet is moving.
The planet you're standing on is racing through space at over eight hundred thousand kilometers an hour.
And somewhere deep below you, it's as hot as the surface of the Sun.
Earth is the only home we've ever known, and it is far stranger than you think.
Here are twelve facts about our planet that sound completely fake, but are one hundred percent true.
And number one sounds like it belongs in a science-fiction movie.
Number twelve. Mount Everest is not the point on Earth that's closest to space.
Because Earth isn't a perfect ball. It spins so fast that it bulges out at the equator.
And that bulge gives a volcano in Ecuador, called Chimborazo, a huge advantage.
Measured from the center of the Earth, its peak sits about two kilometers farther out than the top of Everest.

stat: Chimborazo beats Everest from Earth's center

lines.t: Number eleven. Somewhere on Earth, lightning strikes about forty-four times every second.
That's well over a billion strikes every year.
A single bolt can heat the air around it to around thirty thousand degrees Celsius. That's about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
By the time this video ends, our planet will have been hit by lightning more than fifteen thousand times.
Number ten. The Sahara, the largest hot desert on Earth, was once green.
Around ten thousand years ago, it was covered in grasslands and lakes, home to hippos, giraffes and crocodiles.
And even today, the desert keeps another forest alive.
Every year, millions of tons of Saharan dust blow across the Atlantic Ocean, and fertilize the Amazon rainforest.

sections.head: EVEREST WAS ONCE UNDER THE SEA

lines.t: Number nine. The top of Mount Everest used to be the bottom of the ocean.
Climbers near the summit walk over limestone packed with the fossils of ancient sea creatures.
Hundreds of millions of years ago, that rock was a seafloor.
Then India slammed into Asia, and pushed it nearly nine kilometers into the sky.
Keep that in mind, because number five is genuinely disturbing.
Number eight. The center of the Earth is roughly as hot as the surface of the Sun.
Down there sits a ball of iron and nickel, nearly two and a half thousand kilometers wide.
It's hot enough to melt any metal. But the pressure is so crushing, more than three million times the air pressure you feel right now, that it stays solid.
A ball of solid metal, as hot as the Sun, spinning beneath you right now.
Number seven. Earth's days are getting longer.
The Moon's gravity acts like a brake, slowly dragging on our planet's spin.
About one point four billion years ago, a day on Earth lasted just eighteen hours.

stat: length of a day 1.4 billion years ago

lines.t: And as Earth slows down, the Moon is drifting away from us, about three point eight centimeters every year. That's about as fast as your fingernails grow.

stat: the Moon drifts away every year

lines.t: Number six. Even when you're sitting perfectly still, you're moving incredibly fast.
At the equator, Earth spins at about one thousand six hundred and seventy kilometers an hour.
It orbits the Sun at more than one hundred thousand kilometers an hour.
And our whole solar system is swinging around the galaxy at over eight hundred thousand.
In the time you've spent watching this video, you've already traveled tens of thousands of kilometers.

sections.head: THE LAKE THAT KILLED A VALLEY

lines.t: Number five. In 1986, a lake in Cameroon killed more than seventeen hundred people in a single night.

stat: lives lost in a single night

lines.t: Lake Nyos sits on top of an old volcano, and for years, carbon dioxide had been quietly seeping into its deep water.
Then, one night in August, the lake suddenly released it, all at once.
A massive invisible cloud of gas rolled down into the surrounding valleys, pushing away the oxygen.
Villages went silent. Today, pipes pump gas out of the lake, to stop it from ever building up like that again.

sections.head: WE KNOW MARS BETTER THAN OUR OCEANS

lines.t: Number four. We have better maps of the surface of Mars than we do of our own ocean floor.
Roughly three quarters of the seafloor has never been mapped in high detail.

stat: of the seafloor not mapped in detail

lines.t: The deepest point, the Challenger Deep, is nearly eleven kilometers down.
Drop Mount Everest in there, and its peak would still sit more than two kilometers underwater.
Number three. Earth is slowly leaking into space.
Every day, roughly ninety tons of our atmosphere escape, mostly hydrogen and helium drifting off into the void.
At the same time, space is raining down on us. Tons of cosmic dust and tiny meteors hit our planet every single day.
Don't worry, though. At this rate, our atmosphere will last for billions of years.
Number two. Magnetic north is on the move.
The magnetic north pole has wandered from northern Canada toward Siberia, at times racing more than fifty kilometers a year.

stat: magnetic north moved in a single year

lines.t: And over Earth's history, the magnetic field has completely flipped hundreds of times.
The last full flip happened about seven hundred and eighty thousand years ago. Back then, a compass would have pointed south.

sections.head: A HIDDEN OCEAN INSIDE THE EARTH

lines.t: And number one. There may be a hidden ocean inside the Earth.
Hundreds of kilometers below the surface lies a blue mineral called ringwoodite.
And it can trap water inside its crystal structure.
Scientists estimate that this deep layer of rock could hold as much water as all of Earth's oceans combined... possibly even more.

stat: the water of all oceans, locked in rock

lines.t: Not a liquid sea, but an ocean's worth of water, locked inside stone, right beneath your feet.
So the next time you stand on solid ground, remember. It's moving, it's spinning, it's leaking into space... and it may be hiding an ocean.
And if you think Earth is strange, wait until you see what your own body is doing right now. That video is on your screen. I'll see you there.
